[Penalized Regression: Ridge]{.custom-title}

[Grayson White]{.custom-subtitle} [Stat 243
Week 6 \| Fall 2026]{.custom-subtitle} ::: ::::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Goals for this week :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} ::: {.nonincremental .fragment} **Today:** - Introduce **penalization** to improve MSE in regression models - Define and apply **Ridge Regression** in a case study ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%'} ::: {.nonincremental .fragment} **Next time:** - Introduce **LASSO** as a **penalization and variable selection** method - Apply LASSO in a case study ::: ::: :::: # Penalized Regression ## Recall: Bias-Variance Trade-Off :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="38%"} Bias-Variance Trade-off is useful when selecting among candidate models
::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Linear Regression: + Few predictors (less complex) + Many predictors (more complex) ::: ::: :::: ## Recall: Model Selection Suppose we considered numerous "candidate" models, and picked one using cross-validation: $$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \beta_2X_2 + \epsilon,\qquad \epsilon\sim N(0,~\sigma^2)$$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Next, estimate coefficients using **least-squares** $$\begin{aligned} \text{Find }& \ \hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_2\ \text{ that minimizes }RSS\\ RSS&=\sum_{i=1}^n\Big(Y_i - (\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{1i} + \hat\beta_2X_{2i})\ \Big)^2 \end{aligned}$$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Remember: The model we chose minimized MSE **among the candidate models**: $$\text{MSE} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance}$$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Q:** Could we further lower MSE, **without changing the variables** in our model? ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **A:** Yes! We can change how we **estimate** the coefficients. ::: ## Penalization This week, we're focusing on two **penalization** methods for estimating regression coefficients. ::: {.nonincremental} + Note: "Penalization", "Regularization", and "Shrinkage" are synonyms ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} General Premise: + "Shrink" magnitude of least-squares coefficients ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} + This always *increases bias* $\rightarrow$ **bad!** ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} + Maybe it will *decrease variance a lot* $\rightarrow$ **good!** Overall Effect: **Decrease MSE** (hopefully!) ::: ## Toy Example Suppose we have the following model: $$ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \beta_2X_2 $$ **Least Squares** Regression Coefficients: $$\hat\beta_0 = 2, \ \ \hat\beta_1 = 3, \ \ \hat\beta_2 = 5$$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Two Models: $$\begin{aligned} \text{Least Squares: }&Y = \hat\beta_0 \ + &\hat\beta_1X_1+\ \ \ & \ \ \ \ \hat\beta_2X_2 \\ \text{Shrunken Model: }&Y = \hat\beta_0 \ + &.98\hat\beta_1X_1+\ \ \ &0.95\hat\beta_2X_2 \\ \end{aligned}$$ ::: ## Toy Example: Mathematical Explanation $$\begin{aligned} \text{Least Squares: }&Y = 2 \ + &3X_1+\ \ \ & \ \ \ \ \ 5X_2 \\ \text{Shrunken Model: }&Y = 2 \ + &2.94X_1+\ \ \ &4.75X_2 \\ \end{aligned}$$ Shrunken Model has **higher Bias** than Least Squares -- we modified the coefficients! ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Shrunken Model has **lower Variance** than Least Squares + Recall: $Var(cX) = c^2Var(X)$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} + Intuition: $$\text{Least Squares: }Var(3X_1)=9Var(X_1)$$ ::: ::: {.fragment} $$\text{Shrunken Model: }Var(2.94X_1)=8.64Var(X_1)$$ ::: ::: {.fragment} $$8.64Var(X_1) < 9Var(X_1)$$ ::: ## Toy Example: Simulation Example ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(100) x1 <- runif(20, 0, 1) x2 <- 2 - 2*x1 + rnorm(20, 0, .3) e <- rnorm(20, 0, 1) y <- 1 + x1 + 5*x2 + e data <- data.frame(x1, x2, y) ggplot(data, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = y)) + geom_point(size = 4) + theme_minimal(base_size = 15) + scale_color_viridis_c(option = "B", direction = -1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: We will: ::: {.nonincremental} 1. Split data into training and test sets 2. Fit least squares model to the training data 3. Make predictions on the test data using the "Least Squares" and "Shrunken Models" 4. Compare MSE ::: ## Toy Example: Simulation Example Step 1: Split data into training and test sets ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2) train_indices <- sample(1:20,15) train <- data[train_indices,] test <- data[-train_indices,] ``` ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Step 2: Fit least squares model to the training data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} least_squares <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = train) coef(least_squares) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) x1 x2 0.6764753 1.5186322 5.2849000 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Toy Example: Simulation Example Step 3: Make predictions on the test data using the "Least Squares" and "Shrunken Models" ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ypred_least_squares <- 0.676 + 1.519*test$x1 + 5.285*test$x2 ypred_shrunken_mod <- 0.676 + 0.95*1.519*test$x1 + 0.98*5.285*test$x2 ``` ::: - Could also use the `predict()` function for the least squares model. ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Step 4: Compare MSE ::: {.cell layout-align="center" digits='2'} ```{.r .cell-code} MSE_LeastSquares <- mean( (ypred_least_squares-test$y)^2 ) MSE_ShrunkenMod <- mean( (ypred_shrunken_mod -test$y)^2 ) c(MSE_LeastSquares, MSE_ShrunkenMod) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.3202499 0.2834931 ``` ::: ::: **The shrunken model has lower MSE!** ::: ## When Penalization Works Consider situations where regression has **high MSE:** ::: {.nonincremental} 1) Predictors are **strongly correlated** (high variance) 2) **Many predictors** relative to data size (high variance) 3) Model form is **non-linear** (high bias) ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **To improve models in cases (1) and (2), we could "shrink" coefficients** - Potentially big decreases in variance! - Bias might go up a bit, but maybe that's okay. - Hopefully: MSE decreases overall. ::: ::: {.fragment} **Big Question: How do we actually "shrink" coefficients?** ::: # Ridge Regression ## Ridge Regression $$\text{Regression Model:} \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \dots + \beta_pX_p$$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Least Squares:** Find $\hat\beta$s that minimize $$RSS=\sum_{i=1}^n\Big(Y_i - \underbrace{(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{1i} + \dots + \hat\beta_pX_{pi})}_{\hat Y_i}\ \Big)^2$$ + Goal of RSS: Make regression line "close to data" ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Ridge Regression:** Find $\hat\beta$s that minimize $$ \textrm{RSS} + \underbrace{\lambda\sum_{j = 1}^p \hat\beta_j^2}_\text{Ridge Penalty} \qquad \textrm{where } \lambda \geq 0 \text{ is a set \textbf{tuning parameter}} $$ ::: ## Consider: Effects of the Tuning Parameter, $\lambda$ **Ridge Regression:** Find $\hat\beta$s that minimize $$ \textrm{RSS} + \underbrace{\lambda\sum_{j = 1}^p \hat\beta_j^2}_\text{Ridge Penalty} $$ ::: {.nonincremental} 1. Imagine $\lambda=0$. How do "Ridge" coefficients compare to "Least Squares" coefficients? * [Ridge = Least Squares regression when $\lambda=0$]{.fragment} 2. What happens to $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_p$ as $\lambda$ gets bigger and bigger? * [All $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_p \rightarrow 0$ as $\lambda$ grows.]{.fragment} 3. What happens to $\beta_0$ (intercept) as $\lambda$ gets bigger and bigger? * [$\beta_0 \to \bar{Y}$ as $\lambda$ grows.]{.fragment} ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Note: Effect of Scale Suppose that we find $\hat{Y} = 1 + 5 X_1 + 20 X_2$ using Least Squares. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='45%' .fragment .nonincremental} - Recall: Coefficient Magnitude $\neq$ Importance - Variables may have very different *scales* ::: {.fragment} Coefficients in Least-Squares regression and **scale-equivalent** - If we multiply a predictor ($X_j$) by $2$, then the resulting coefficient ($\hat{\beta}_j$) would be multiplied by $1/2$. ::: ::: ::: {.column width='10%'} ::: ::: {.column width='45%' .fragment .nonincremental} In **Ridge Regression**, coefficients can change depending on scale! - Variables with bigger scales are penalized more. Software solves this problem: - Variables are "standardized" - Ridge Regression performed on standardized variables - Coefficients are re-scaled to the original scale. ::: :::: # Case Study: Molecule Solubility ## Molecular Solubility **Data:** Chemical properties for $n$=285 compounds ::: {.nonincremental} - **Response, $Y$:** *log(Solubility)*. Solubility is how easily a compound dissolves in a solvent. - **Predictors, $X$:** $p=20$ chemical properties, such as "number of bromine atoms" or "molecular weight". ::: **Goal:** Model solubility based on these 20 chemical descriptors. ## Data preprocessing and EDA ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column-fragment'} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1-13|15-22"} library(AppliedPredictiveModeling) data(solubility) # Data preprocessing solTest <- data.frame(solTestX, Solubility = solTestY) solTrain <- data.frame(solTrainX, Solubility = solTrainY) solTest <- solTest %>% select(!starts_with("FP")) solTrain <- solTrain %>% select(!starts_with("FP")) # Considering a smaller training set (30% of original size) set.seed(1) solTrain <- solTrain %>% sample_frac(.3) # Plotting solTrain %>% ggplot(aes(x = Solubility)) + geom_histogram(color = "white", fill = "steelblue") + labs(title = "Distribution of Y (Log Solubility)", x = "Log Solubility") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Pairwise Scatterplots ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} solTrain %>% pivot_longer(-Solubility, names_to = "var", values_to = "value") %>% ggplot(aes(x = value, y = Solubility)) + geom_point(alpha = .15, shape = 16) + geom_smooth(se = F, color = "maroon", linewidth = .35) + facet_wrap( ~ var, nrow = 5, scales = "free") + theme_bw() + labs(y = "Log(Solubility)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Least Squares Consider the **least squares** model fit to our data. $$Y = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_1 + \dots + \hat\beta_{20}X_{20}$$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Suppose we have a **test set** to evaluate our model, consisting of (new) 316 compounds. + We compute test MSE: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} full_mod <- lm(Solubility ~ ., data = solTrain) preds <- predict(full_mod, solTest) mean((solTest$Solubility - preds)^2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.9921199 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Ridge Regression in `R` ::: {.nonincremental} Can we reduce the test MSE by "shrinking" the coefficients? + Let's re-fit our model using several different values of $\lambda$... ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1-4|6|8-13"} # [,-1] removes the first column of this matrix, in this case, # it is the intercept. We don't want to penalize the intercept! x <- model.matrix(Solubility ~., data = solTrain)[,-1] y <- solTrain$Solubility grid <- 10^(seq(-5, 3, length = 100)) library(glmnet) # fits ridge regression models ridge_mod <- glmnet(x = x, y = y, # alpha = 0 specifies "ridge" alpha = 0, lambda = grid) ``` ::: ::: ## Ridge Coefficient Estimates, by $\lambda$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(ridge_mod, sign.lambda = 1, label = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: **Q:** What happens to coefficient size as $\lambda$ changes? **Q:** Why do some coefficients change sign as $\lambda$ changes? ## Ridge Coefficient Estimates, by $\lambda$ with `ggplot2` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(broom) tidied <- tidy(ridge_mod) %>% filter(term != "(Intercept)") ggplot(tidied, aes(lambda, estimate, group = term, color = term)) + geom_line() + scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10^c(-5, -3, 0, 3)), labels = c(".00001", ".001", "1", "1000")) + theme_bw(base_size = 10) + labs(y = "Coefficent estimate", color = "Predictor", x = expression(lambda~" ('lambda')")) + guides(color = guide_legend(ncol = 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## How do we select $\lambda$? **Q:** How do we find the **best** value of $\lambda$? ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **A: Cross-validation!** - Compare test MSE between models fit using different values of $\lambda$ - Select $\lambda$ that minimizes the test MSE - This model represents an "optimal" relationship between bias and variance ::: ## Cross-Validation Estimate of Test MSE (10-fold CV) ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column-fragment'} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="3-7|9-16"} set.seed(1010) # Cross validation with glmnet my_cv <- cv.glmnet(x = x, y = y, alpha = 0, lambda = grid, nfolds = 10) # Plotting results tidied <- tidy(my_cv) ggplot(tidied, aes(x = lambda, y = estimate)) + geom_line(color = "red") + scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10^c(-5, -3, 0, 3)), labels = c(".00001", ".001", "1", "1000")) + theme_bw(base_size = 15) + labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Test MSE") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Zooming In ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} tidied %>% filter(lambda <= 1e-03 & lambda >= 1e-5) %>% ggplot(aes(x = lambda, y = estimate)) + geom_line(color = "red") + scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10^c(-5:-3)), labels = c(".00001", ".0001", ".001")) + theme_bw(base_size = 15) + labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Test MSE") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.nonincremental} + Test MSE is minimized at **0.8841** when $\lambda = 0.0001$ + Recall: Original model had Test MSE = **0.992**. **Ridge Regression improved predictive performance!** ::: ## Recap ::: {.nonincremental} Today, we learned about... - Shrinking coefficients to increase bias, but lower variance and MSE - Ridge Regression as one type of penalization **Next Time**: - Introduce **LASSO** as a **penalization and variable selection** method - Apply LASSO in a case study :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
